newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMAN BUILDERS SEE RECESSION DRAGGING ON IN '97.
newsitem.headline: GERMAN BUILDERS SEE RECESSION DRAGGING ON IN '97.

text.p: Germany's construction industry will remain depressed in 1997 and shed a further 60,000 workers after faltering badly over the past year, the head of the BI builders federation said on Monday.

"We can hope for stabilisation in 1998 at the earliest," Heiko Stiepelmann told a news conference. The building sector is set to end 1997 employing 1.25 million workers after losing 100,000 workers last year.
Stiepelmann said he expected building investment to fall by a real 1.4 percent this year in western Germany and by five percent in the former communist east.
In the year just ended, building investment fell by three percent in the west and by 1.7 percent in eastern Germany.

Weak construction activity turned out to be a major brake on German growth last year, and some forecasters say that a slowdown in the ex-communist east following a post-unification boom could lead the region into recession.
Whether the building sector will be able to stabilise hangs on Germany hitting the official economic growth forecast of 2.5 percent this year, Stiepelmann said.

One key think tank on a government forecasting panel, the Berlin-based DIW institute, has already distanced itself from the official view and predicted slower growth in gross domestic product of two percent for 1997.
Stiepelmann also said that government plans for a major tax reform was also raising concerns in the construction sector over the outlook for housebuilding.
And he added he hoped that government cutbacks in building spending to ensure that Germany meets tough borrowing targets to qualify for European would slacken off in 1998.

Spending on homebuilding, which accounts for around a half of total building investment, is expected by the BI to fall by 1.7 percent this year. Broken down, the fall would be four percent in the east and one percent in western Germany.

Commercial construction, which makes up around 30 percent of the total, is seen falling by 2.4 percent this year. In the west, the fall is seen at around one percent, while in eastern Germany the slide will be more pronounced at five percent.

Public construction investment -- the area hit hardest by government savings efforts last year -- is also seen shrinking this year by three percent. The fall is seen at four percent in the west and by three percent in the east, the BI said.
